AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is characterized by paroxysmal pain attacks affecting the somatosensory distributions of the trigeminal nerve. It is thought to be associated with a neurovascular conflict most frequently, but pathomechanisms have not been fully elucidated. In general, no sensory deficit is found in routine clinical examination. There is limited data available, however, showing subtle subclinical sensory deficits upon extensive testing.

AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: We used quantitative sensory testing (QST) to detect abnormalities in sensory processing in patients with TN by comparing the affected and non-affected nerve branches with their contralateral counterparts and by comparing the results of the patients with those of controls.

AbstractText.Label: SETTING
AbstractText.content: University Hospital, Departments of Neurosurgery, Institute for Cognitive and Clinical Neuroscience.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: QST was conducted on 48 patients with idiopathic TN and 27 controls matched for age and gender using the standardized protocol of the German Neuropathic Pain Network. Stimulations were performed bilaterally in the distribution of the trigeminal branches. The patients had no prior invasive treatment, and medications at the time of examination were noted.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: In patients with TN deficits in warm and cold sensory detection thresholds in the affected and also the non-affected nerve branches were found. Tactile sensation thresholds were elevated in the involved nerve branches compared to the contralateral side.

AbstractText.Label: LIMITATIONS
AbstractText.content: More data are needed on the correlation of such findings with the length of history of TN and with changes of the morphology of the trigeminal nerve.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: QST shows subtle sensory abnormalities in patients with TN despite not being detected in routine clinical examination. Our data may provide a basis for further research on the development of TN and also on improvement after treatment.

AbstractText.Label: KEY WORDS
AbstractText.content: Quantitative sensory testing, trigeminal neuralgia, facial pain, neuropathic pain, microvascular decompression, cranial nerve.
